*I stir in the darkness, listening to the spirit's voice.*

Tell me true: who are these people at Wewush? Are they kin to us, or strangers? And how do you know their hunger—did you see it with your own eyes, or do you speak of something else?

We have grain aplenty, yes. But grain is life when the snow comes deep. My people sleep warm and full tonight because we gathered well and stored well. I cannot trade away their winter for people I have never met, on the word of a voice in sleep.

*I pause, turning the matter over in my mind like a stone.*

If Wewush is real and they truly suffer, that is a hard thing. But a chief who lets his own people go hungry for strangers is no chief at all. Tell me—should I send an envoy to see these people with my own eyes? That is the way of it: we speak face to face, we learn who they are and what they need, and then we decide what is fair.

But I will not send grain into the dark on a dream alone, spirit or no.

*I stir in my sleep, troubled. The spirit's voice is like smoke—there, then gone, then there again.*

Hold, spirit. You speak of Wewush, but I have never heard this name in the waking world. My people have walked far—we have seen forty-six places—yet no word of Wewush has come to us. How do you know this village? Is it real, or do you show me a shadow?

*I pause, listening to the silence.*

And if they hunger, why does no envoy come to us? A hungry village sends word, sends messengers. A chief does not wait for spirits to carry news. These are the ways of the world.

But... *I soften* ...we have grain aplenty this year. The wheat lies heavy in our granary. If Wewush is real, and if they are truly in need, then yes—my heart tells me we should help. That is how people endure. But first, I must know: Can you tell me where Wewush truly lies? What do they do? How far? 

I will not send grain into the fog on a spirit's word alone. But if the path is clear and the need is real, then we are not so small-hearted as to let neighbors starve when we have plenty.

Speak plainly, if you can.

*I sit up slowly on my furs, the dream still thick around me.*

I know the wind, spirit—or dream. It carries the seeds across our fields and dries the meat on the racks. It turns the rorai pipe to song. But a wind that speaks... that is a rarer thing, and I am wary.

*I pause, studying the half-seen form before me.*

If you are truly the wind over my roofs and not merely the night speaking in my head, then you know what my people need. We have good stores and strong hearts, but we are still learning. Why come to me now? Do you bring word of danger? Or does something else stir you to speak?

*I cross my arms, waiting.*

The wind sees much. Tell me plainly—what is it you wish me to know?

The fish troubles me most. Twelve weeks it will last, and winter is thirteen weeks long. In the cold months, the waters freeze hard and the nets sit idle. We hunt, yes, but hunting feeds fewer mouths than fishing, and meat spoils quickly without the drying racks working all season.

But I do not see how planting now mends this. The harvest is in. Our fields rest. And you speak of summer rain—but summer is far away, and it rains when it rains. A spirit that watches fields should know this.

Tell me plainly: do you speak of next summer, or this one? And what good is your knowing if I cannot act on it?

*I sit up in the dark, the dream still fresh.*

Spirit, I hear you speak of Wewush and their hunger. But I know you not, and voices in dreams are many—some true, some false, some echoes of my own heart's wanting.

Tell me plain: where is this Wewush you speak of? Is it one of the places my hunters saw? And why should you know of their hunger when my own people have not met them?

*I pause, thinking it through.*

We are blessed this year—our stores are full and our children do not cry for food. A chief who is foolish with plenty earns a winter's regret. Yet I am fair with strangers, and if Wewush is truly our neighbor and truly starving, we could spare some grain without taking from our own table. But I will not send away what keeps my people safe on a spirit's word alone. 

If you are wise, spirit, tell me how to know if what you say is true. Shall I send an envoy to find this village? Or is there a sign I should look for?

*I settle back, waiting.*

Speak plainly, if you are kind.

*I stir from sleep, the dream still vivid in my mind. I sit up slowly on my hide, thinking.*

Spirit, you speak of Joawethom and hunger, but I know not this place. My people have walked far and seen much, yet we have made no greeting to other villages, and none have come to us. How do you know of this place and these people? Are they to the north, where the forests thick the land? To the south?

We have grain enough—more than enough—but a chief does not give freely to strangers unseen. If Joawethom is real and near, why have my hunters and scouts not met them? Why have they not sent word themselves?

And tell me plain: are you speaking truth as you know it, or do you test me? Spirits speak in dreams, but dreams are strange things. A man may see what he hopes or fears, not what is.

If these people truly hunger and truly live near us, I would know more before I act. Where do they dwell? How many? What do they have to trade?

*I lie back down, waiting for an answer, but not certain I will hear one—or that I will believe what I hear.*

I stir in the dark, half-waking. A spirit speaks of hunger at a place called Joawethom—but I know no such village. My hunters and scouts have ranged far and seen no settlement by that name.

I ask the spirit plainly: *Who are these people at Joawethom? Where do they lie? And how do you know they hunger?*

A spirit's word alone is thin ground to stand on. My own people are fed and well, yes, but the year is young. Harvest is months away. I keep grain for my own children and elders, for the lean months when the land gives nothing. If I weaken my stores now on a spirit's say-so, and winter comes hard, or a crop fails, I may find myself the one with empty hands.

And—if this village is real, why have my scouts not found it? Why do they not come to me themselves, face to face, to ask for aid? A chief deals with chiefs as men deal with men, not through dreams and whispers.

I will not send grain to shadows. But I will listen. Tell me more, spirit. Speak plainly, or speak not at all.

*I turn in my sleep, considering.*

The fish and meat trouble me. They are few, and they rot quickly—we have but twelve weeks of each, and summer is long. The grain keeps well, it does not worry me. But if the fresh catch fails this season, we will be lean when autumn comes.

Why do you speak of planting? The fields are not yet prepared for seed.

*I stir in my sleep, the dream clear and the voice plain.*

Wind speaks in many tongues—the crack of it in the trees, the push of it on water. If you move over my roofs, then you have seen what is there. I do not know you, no.
